power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p-value <0.10", "p=0.43", "p=0.23"), Sentence = c("Because the direction of effect was prespecified, this corresponds to a two-sided p-value <0.10/k, specifically p<0.0062 for species and p<0.00323 for KEGG.", "Similar estimates were observed with the weighted median Mendelian randomization approach, and there was no evidence of directional pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept p=0.43), no heterogeneity (Cochran's Q p=0.23), and no outlier variants detected by MR-PRESSO (Supplementary Table 13).", "Similar estimates were observed with the weighted median Mendelian randomization approach, and there was no evidence of directional pleiotropy (MR-Egger intercept p=0.43), no heterogeneity (Cochran's Q p=0.23), and no outlier variants detected by MR-PRESSO (Supplementary Table 13)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background: The gut microbiome is an emerging risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD).

Methods: We tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across four large prospective Nordic cohorts with 635 incident CVD in 11,604 participants in the discovery cohort and 2,309 incident CVD in 20,965 participants combined across three replication cohorts.
Results: Higher Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a lower risk of incident CVD.

In addition, the relative abundance of nine species and eleven bacterial functional modules showed reproducible associations with incident CVD in the discovery cohort and in a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts.

We identified a femalespecific gut microbiota-related pathway involving the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, enriched among denture users, thus serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal effect of denture use on increased relative abundance of Rothia mucilaginosa_A.

This pathway was linked to increased CVD risk through altered gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating imidazole propionate levels, and increased levels of systemic inflammation biomarkers.

The second pathway involved both α-diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of metabolic syndrome and with bacterial pathways related to purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis.
Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways provide new insights into the underlying biology of CVD.
Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and cardiovascular disease may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

text.text: Briefly, 56,042 individuals participated in HUNT4 (2017-2019) and 13,268 provided stool samples. 50% of these have participated in all HUNT surveys.
After sequencing and quality control, 12,887 individuals were included in this analysis.
Samples were processed, and deep metagenomic sequencing was performed by Cmbio (Copenhagen, Denmark; previously named Clinical Microbiomics A/S).
Three circular punches (6 mm diameter) were taken from each stool collection card and placed into designated wells of MagMAX™ 96 Deep Well Plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).

Microbial cells were lysed by bead beating, after which DNA was purified using the MagMAX Ultra Microbiome kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions on a KingFisher™ Flex instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
DNA was enzymatically fragmented and sequencing libraries were generated using the Celero EZ DNA-seq Core Module on a Tecan DreamPrep NGS automated platform.

Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 system with paired-end 150 bp reads, producing an average depth of 22.9 million read pairs per sample with more than 85% of bases achieving a Phred quality score above 30.
Metagenomics methodology in SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and FINRISK is described in the Supplementary Methods.

Briefly, for SCAPIS, metagenomic sequencing using the Illumina Novaseq 6000 system yielded an average sequence depth of 25.3 million read pairs for the Uppsala samples and 26.3 million read pairs for Malmö samples.
For SIMPLER, sequencing on MGI DNBSEQ G400 or T7 platforms generated an average of 51 million reads per sample.
For FINRISK, sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform yielded an average of 900,000 reads per sample.

For species and KEGG modules, we considered a finding to be replicated if the meta-analysis estimate had the same direction of effect as the discovery analysis and reached significance in a one-sided test at a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of α =0.05/k where k is the number of features tested.

text.text: Among 11,604 participants in the HUNT discovery cohort, we identified 635 incident CVD cases (5%) during a median follow-up of 5.2 years.

The incidence of CVD differed across the three replication cohorts, with the highest incidence observed in SIMPLER (935 cases; 18%) and FINRISK (1,157 cases; 17%), reflecting the higher baseline age in SIMPLER and the longer follow-up time in FINRISK, whereas the lowest incidence was observed in SCAPIS (217 cases; 2%), attributable to its lower baseline age, shorter follow-up time, and the omission of heart failure from the CVD definition (Table 1).

text.text: In the HUNT study, each standard deviation (SD) increase in the Shannon diversity index was associated with a 9% lower hazard of CVD (HR=0.91; 95% CI 0.84-0.99).
Similarly, higher species richness was associated with a lower risk of CVD (HR=0.91; 95% CI 0.84-0.99).

In a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and FINRISK; Table 2, Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Figure 1), increases in both the Shannon diversity index (HR=0.90; 95% CI 0.86-0.94) and species richness (HR=0.88; 95% CI 0.85-0.92) were associated with a reduced hazard of incident CVD, with effect estimates closely mirroring those observed in HUNT.

text.text: This pattern suggests that a distinct biological pathway, rather than traditional metabolic syndrome-related pathways, may underlie the link between this species and increased risk of CVD.

text.text: Thus, microbial features consistently associated with incident CVD remain insufficiently defined.
In the present study, we examined stool-derived metagenomes within a discovery-replication framework across four large Nordic cohorts (N=32,569; n=2,944 incident CVD events across the four cohorts).
We identified the first gut microbiome features reproducibly associated with incident CVD, including two indices of α-diversity, nine species, and eleven functional KEGG modules.
We observed two main pathways for these associations between the gut microbiome and incident CVD.

The first pathway involved the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, linking it to increased incident CVD risk through affected gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating ImP, and systemic inflammation, and this relationship appeared to be female-specific.
The second pathway involved -diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, which were strongly linked to metabolic syndrome.
Collectively, these results highlight two principal pathways through which the gut microbiome may be linked to CVD (Figure 4).

Furthermore, the abundance of the functional KEGG module for manganese transport system, which was strongly correlated with Rothia mucilaginosa_A, was also linked to increased risk of incident CVD specifically in females, while showing no associations with metabolic-syndromerelated parameters.

text.text: The second pattern linked incident CVD to gut microbiome parameters, including α-diversity metrics and eight species which were also strongly linked to multiple metabolic-syndrome markers in the expected direction.

Low α-diversity, reflected by reduced Shannon diversity index and species richness, was associated with a higher risk of CVD as well as elevated waist-to-hip ratio, systolic blood pressure, triglycerides, HbA1c, and CRP.
These are characteristic features of the metabolic syndrome which is closely linked to increased cardiovascular risk 67, 68 .

text.text: This metabolic syndrome-associated pathway was also associated with several functional gut microbiota-associated pathways reflecting purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis.

Our observation that lower Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a higher risk of incident CVD aligns with prior cross-sectional findings from the Framingham Heart Study, demonstrating that decreased gut microbiota α-diversity was associated with an increased calculated 10-year risk of CVD 3 .
We also observed that low α-diversity was associated with high CRP, reflecting systemic inflammation.

Collectively, these findings underscore that reduced gut microbiota α-diversity, a signature of the metabolic syndrome and an unstable and inflammation-prone gut ecosystem, marks increased cardiovascular risk.

text.text: These associations for functional KEGG modules with incident CVD suggest gut microbial features that may promote low-grade chronic inflammation, providing a biological basis for atherosclerotic plaque progression and thrombosis and thereby contributing to CVD.
We observed that increased relative abundance of Mediterraneibacter torques was associated with increased risk of CVD and was significantly positively correlated with all tested metabolic parameters.
This is consistent with previous studies linking Mediterraneibacter torques to high blood pressure and adiposity 73, 74 .

text.text: In addition, Mediterraneibacter torques is a specialist in mucin degradation and has been associated with intestinal inflammation, potentially driven by increased gut permeability resulting from reduced mucin-protective layers, thereby promoting immune activation and systemic inflammation.
Our study has several strengths.
It is by far the largest investigation conducted to date and includes a successful replication phase with complete follow-up enabled through linkage to high-quality Nordic registers.
We used metagenomic sequencing rather than 16S rRNA gene sequencing, which enables species-level resolution and functional characterization.
Because we were able to perform sensitivity analyses accounting for diet as well as proton pump inhibitor and antibiotic use, we could adjust for notable confounders.
Finally, our study was conducted in populations with deep phenotyping, enabling the investigation of potential underlying mechanisms.
Our findings should be interpreted in the context of the study limitations.
First, our analysis only indicates microbiome features correlated with, but not necessarily causal for, CVD.
We rely on diagnosis codes from hospitals and death registries, rather than validated outcomes, which may be imperfect and result in misclassification.
Furthermore, only prescribed medications are captured in the prescription databases, so the binary PPI exposure variable may underestimate true PPI usage.
Although metagenomic sequencing allows species-level resolution, some disease-causing metabolic activities of the gut microbiome may exist at the strain level, which we were unable to account for.
Residual confounding by unmeasured factors or by imprecise measurement of adjusted covariates such as self-reported diet, remains possible.
Finally, our findings may not be generalizable to other global populations outside of the Nordic region.
The use of the CVD outcome has advantages and disadvantages.
The composite CVD outcome combines cardiovascular outcomes with partially distinct pathophysiology.
While myocardial infarction and stroke are closely related to atherothrombosis and plaque instability, heart failure reflects more heterogeneous mechanisms, from arrhythmias to valvular disease.
However, the composite CVD endpoint is frequently used in randomized clinical trials, so our findings are informative for future interventional studies.
In addition, combining the cardiovascular outcomes into a composite outcome likely aided in statistical power to identify associations.
While the CVD definition was harmonized across cohorts, there was some heterogeneity, for example, data for heart failure was not available for SCAPIS.
In conclusion, we identified gut microbiome features reproducibly associated with incident CVD.
We observed two main pathways for these associations between gut microbiota and incident CVD.
The first pathway was female-specific and involved the oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, which was enriched among denture users, serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health.
This pathway linked Rothia mucilaginosa_A to increased incident CVD risk through altered manganese transport, elevated circulating ImP levels, and heightened systemic inflammation.

text.text: The second more general pathway involved -diversity metrics and eight species, which were strongly associated with multiple markers of the metabolic syndrome.

These findings indicate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways may provide new insights into the etiology of CVD and may ultimately help guide its prevention and treatment.
Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and CVD may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

Gut microbial species and functional KEGG modules associated with incident CVD in discovery and replication cohorts (A) Estimated effect sizes for the 9 replicated metagenomic species in the HUNT study (discovery) and a fixed-effect meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting of the replication cohorts SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and FINRISK.

text.text: Figure 4.

Proposed pathways underlying the association between gut microbiota and incident CVD Two main proposed pathways for the link between gut microbiota and incident CVD.Associations linked to increased risk of CVD are in blue and decreased risk of CVD are in purple.
A first female-specific pathway involves Rothia mucilaginosa_A, a prevalent oral gut microbiota species, which was enriched among denture users, serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health.
This species is linked to increased risk of incident CVD through affected gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating concentrations of imidazole propionate and systemic inflammation.

The second pathway involves α-diversity metrics and eight replicated species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of the metabolic syndrome, an established major determinant of incident CVD.
